data.title: Alphabet (GOOGL) Q3 earnings preview: US$200 billion AI capex test puts major uptrend at risk
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key takeaways

  • Google Cloud is the key growth catalyst, but investors will watch whether rapid AI-driven revenue expansion is matched by healthy margins and cash generation.
  • Capex and free cash flow are the biggest valuation risks, especially if Alphabet raises spending again without clearer evidence of improving AI returns.
  • Technically, 359.44 is the key resistance, while a break below 300.44 may expose 270.70 and signal a deeper deterioration in the major uptrend.

Ahead of Wednesday’s Q3 2026 earnings, Alphabet (GOOGL) faces a critical test of whether surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing can sustain its rapid Google Cloud growth while offsetting mounting concerns over infrastructure spending, free cash flow and profitability.

Alphabet is expected to release its Q3 results after the US market closes on Wednesday, 28 October 2026, with its earnings conference call scheduled for 4:30 pm Eastern Time.

Based on the street’s expectations, there is an underlying divergence: revenue is expected to increase by nearly 25% year-on-year to US$127.92B, but EPS growth is projected at just 5.6% year-on-year to US$3.02.

Highlighting the market’s focus on whether AI infrastructure costs are beginning to dilute underlying earnings growth. EPS comparisons also require care because Alphabet’s Q2 results included unusually large investment-related gains.

Following weakness in AI-linked technology stocks since the start of October, investors are increasingly questioning whether aggressive capital expenditure commitments will generate sufficient returns to justify elevated valuations.

Alphabet’s shares recorded a loss of 6.34% from the start of October through 26 October 2026, reflecting broader weakness in AI-related technology stocks, with juggernaut Nvidia and the US PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index declining by 6.44% and 13.61% respectively (see Fig. 1).

Ahead of Alphabet’s Q3 earnings release, options markets are pricing an approximately ±6.0% move in Alphabet’s (GOOGL) shares as of 26 October 2026, almost on par with its 10-year average peak earnings-day movement of 6.6%, according to data from EarningsWatcher.

Against this backdrop, Alphabet’s earnings reaction is likely to hinge on six key fundamentals.

1. Google Cloud: the most important earnings growth catalyst

Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year on year to US$24.8 billion in Q2 2026, driven by enterprise AI infrastructure, enterprise AI solutions and core cloud services. Cloud growth significantly outpaced the wider group’s 24% revenue expansion. [1]

Importantly, Cloud has become Alphabet’s clearest avenue for monetising the AI infrastructure boom, benefiting from rising demand for Google Cloud Platform, Gemini-related workloads and its proprietary Tensor Processing Units (TPUs).

J.P. Morgan recently raised its Alphabet price target from US$420 to US$425, expecting Google Cloud’s Q3 revenue to approximately double from the same period a year ago.

2. Google Search advertising: can AI strengthen rather than undermine its core business?

Google Search remains Alphabet’s largest profit engine and an important source of funding for its capital-intensive AI expansion.

In Q2, Google Services revenue increased 15% year on year to US$94.5 billion, supported by 17% growth in Google Search and other advertising revenue, while YouTube advertising revenue increased 13%.

Traders will likely focus on whether AI-powered Search experiences, including AI Overviews and Gemini integration, are driving higher engagement and commercial search activity without undermining traditional advertising monetisation.

The market is particularly sensitive to whether conversational AI services divert users from conventional search queries and reduce the number of profitable advertising opportunities.

3. Capital expenditure and free cash flow: the biggest valuation risk

Alphabet raised its full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance by US$15 billion to US$195 billion–US$205 billion following its Q2 earnings, reflecting accelerated investment in AI computing, data centres and network infrastructure.

The spending increase comes amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment cycle. In the first six months of 2026 alone, Alphabet recorded US$80.6 billion in capital expenditure, compared with US$39.6 billion during the same period in 2025. [2]

Of particular concern, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of approximately US$5.9 billion in Q2 despite strong revenue growth.

Traders will focus on three questions: whether 2026 spending guidance will increase again, whether management expects another substantial rise in 2027, and whether AI-generated revenue can eventually outpace growth in infrastructure costs.

4. Operating margins: Is AI growth translating into higher profitability?

Alphabet’s Q2 operating income rose 30% year on year, with its operating margin expanding by two percentage points to 34%.

However, rising depreciation, energy requirements, personnel expenses, and infrastructure costs could gradually erode operating leverage as new data-centre capacity comes online.

Investors will closely monitor Google Cloud operating profitability alongside Alphabet’s consolidated operating margin to determine whether the rapid expansion in AI-related revenue is translating into sustainable earnings growth.

A further complication is Alphabet’s investment-related gains. Q2 reported EPS of US$9.11 was significantly boosted by non-operating investment gains, while underlying EPS excluding those gains was approximately US$2.85.

5. Gemini, TPUs and enterprise AI monetisation

Beyond the headline Cloud revenue numbers, investors will assess whether Alphabet’s vertically integrated AI strategy is generating a sustainable competitive advantage.

Alphabet’s proprietary TPU infrastructure provides an alternative to Nvidia GPUs, while Gemini models and enterprise AI services offer additional monetisation opportunities across Google Cloud, Workspace and consumer products.

In Q2, Alphabet began recognising revenue from direct TPU sales, while its Cloud order backlog reportedly reached US$514 billion.

This creates an important potential growth driver; Alphabet can benefit not only from operating its own AI infrastructure but also from supplying computing capacity and specialised hardware to external customers.

6. Forward guidance and macroeconomic conditions

Alphabet reports during a period of elevated uncertainty surrounding US interest rates, inflation and the sustainability of AI infrastructure investment.

The recent weakness in technology and semiconductor stocks has been amplified by concerns over higher Treasury yields and the potential for additional Federal Reserve tightening.

This environment creates two distinct risks for Alphabet.

First, higher interest rates increase the discount rate applied to future earnings, potentially weighing on valuation multiples even if its operational performance remains strong.

Second, persistent inflation and higher energy prices could raise data-centre operating costs while dampening corporate advertising budgets and enterprise technology spending.

At the same time, a resilient US economy and sustained enterprise investment in AI could provide an offsetting tailwind for both Google Search advertising and Google Cloud.

Share-price implication: Strong fourth-quarter guidance, continued advertising resilience, and confident AI spending commentary could support a recovery in Alphabet’s shares. Conversely, weaker advertising demand, accelerating infrastructure costs, or more cautious management commentary could reinforce recent selling pressure across AI-related technology stocks.

Fundamental bottom line: what matters most for traders

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings reaction will likely hinge on four key factors: Google Cloud growth, Search advertising resilience, AI capital expenditure and operating margin performance, with forward guidance playing a decisive role in determining the stock’s post-earnings direction.

The bull case is clean earnings beat, accelerating Google Cloud revenue growth, resilient Search advertising demand and improving AI monetisation, supported by stable capital expenditure guidance and healthy operating margins.

This would reinforce Alphabet’s competitive advantage in AI infrastructure and potentially trigger further valuation expansion.

The bear case is not necessarily disappointing headline earnings, but signs that AI infrastructure spending is rising faster than revenue and profitability.

Slowing Cloud growth, weaker Search monetisation, margin compression or another substantial increase in 2027 capital expenditure expectations may trigger selling pressure, particularly amid heightened scrutiny of AI investment returns.

Let’s now focus on the medium-term outlook of Alphabet’s share price from a technical analysis perspective.

Technical analysis: Major uptrend in jeopardy

Since printing its current all-time intraday high of 408.61 on 18 May 2026, Alphabet (GOOGL) has staged a corrective decline of 22.9%, hitting a low of 314.90 on 23 July 2026.

Recent price action in GOOGL suggests that the bears are likely in control, and it faces an increasing risk of a breakdown from its current major uptrend phase, in place since the 7 April 2025 low of 140.53 (see Fig. 2).

GOOGL has staged a bearish breakdown below its 50- and 200-day moving averages.

In addition, the volatility-adjusted relative strength (VARS) of GOOGL against the Nasdaq 100 exchange-traded fund (QQQ) has trended downward since 16 October 2026, indicating further potential underperformance of GOOGL relative to the Nasdaq 100.

Watch the 359.44 key medium-term pivotal resistance to maintain the bearish bias for GOOGL; a break below 300.44 support (also the lower boundary of the major ascending channel) may trigger another potential multi-week corrective down move to expose the next medium-term support at 270.70 in the first step.

On the other hand, a clearance and a daily close above 359.44 would invalidate the bearish bias, with the next medium-term resistance at 383.00, before a potential retest of the current all-time intraday high of 408.61.

data.title: The US labour market is losing momentum – as is the USD
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • The U.S. labor market is losing momentum, but not collapsing. Nonfarm payrolls rose by only 57,000, previous months were revised lower, and hiring has clearly slowed, while layoffs remain limited.
  • The drop in unemployment is less positive than it looks. The unemployment rate fell to 4.2%, but this was partly due to a decline in labor force participation to 61.5%, meaning some people stopped actively looking for work.
  • The report reduced pressure on the Fed to tighten policy further. Slower job growth and easing wage pressure revived hopes for future rate cuts, weakened the dollar, and supported assets such as gold, Bitcoin, and EUR/USD.

June data from the U.S. labor market showed a clear weakening in employment momentum. Nonfarm payrolls increased by only 57,000, significantly below economists’ expectations. In addition, data for the previous two months were revised downward, weakening earlier signals that had suggested greater resilience in the labor market.

At first glance, the decline in the unemployment rate to 4.2% appeared positive. However, this is not an unambiguous sign of improvement. The drop in unemployment was accompanied by a marked decline in labor force participation. The participation rate fell to 61.5%, reaching its lowest level in more than five years. This means that some individuals stopped actively looking for work and were therefore no longer included in unemployment statistics.

Companies are not conducting mass layoffs, but they are hiring more cautiously

The report does not point to a labor market collapse, but it does show increasing caution among employers. Initial jobless claims remained almost unchanged, suggesting that the scale of layoffs remains limited. The issue, therefore, is not a sharp reduction in employment, but a weaker willingness among companies to create new jobs.

The largest decline in employment was recorded in the leisure and hospitality sector. This is particularly important because, at this time of year, the industry typically increases seasonal hiring. Weaker-than-usual employment growth may indicate a more cautious approach by companies toward consumer demand and future operating costs.

At the same time, some sectors continued to support the labor market. Healthcare and social assistance remained the main source of employment growth. Job numbers also increased in manufacturing and construction. Weakness persisted, however, in the information sector, where employment declined for the seventeenth time in the past eighteen months.

Wages are rising, but inflationary pressure is easing

Average hourly earnings rose by 3.5% year over year in June. This increase shows that wages are still growing, but they are no longer generating inflationary pressure as strong as during the period of peak labor market tightness. For the Federal Reserve, this may be an argument that employment conditions remain relatively stable and do not require an abrupt policy response.

From the perspective of households, however, the picture is less favorable. Slower employment growth means fewer opportunities to find a new job, while inflation continues to limit the real purchasing power of wages. Even if nominal wages are rising, many workers may not feel a clear improvement in their financial situation.

Markets took note of the report’s weakness

The release triggered a moderately positive reaction in financial markets. The S&P 500 opened higher, while U.S. Treasury yields declined. Investors scaled back expectations for further interest rate hikes by the Fed, although they still priced in at least one rate increase this year.

The market reaction shows that weaker employment data were interpreted as a factor reducing pressure on the central bank. If the labor market continues to lose momentum, the Fed may have fewer reasons to tighten monetary policy further.

A mixed picture of the U.S. economy

The data were disappointing, but they should not fundamentally change the overall assessment of the economy. The labor market reflects uneven economic growth, in which some sectors are still creating jobs while others are clearly slowing. From the Fed’s perspective, the situation does not look alarming, as the labor market is not generating additional inflationary pressure. For American households, however, it means more difficult conditions, especially when limited employment opportunities coincide with persistently high living costs.

Kevin Warsh’s first press conference as FOMC Chair was perceived as hawkish and fueled concerns about an interest rate hike in the United States. As a result, the dollar strengthened significantly in recent weeks. Following today’s NFP report, hopes for an interest rate cut have resurfaced. Of course, with core PCE inflation currently at 3.4% year over year, this remains unlikely. Nevertheless, today’s reading creates a balance between arguments for monetary easing and monetary tightening, given the Fed’s dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability. It was precisely these hopes that led to a weakening of the dollar. EUR/USD is currently trading at 1.1446, up 0.59%. Instruments quoted in USD, which have recently failed to generate returns for investors, also deserve attention. Gold is up 2.37% today, while Bitcoin has gained 2.64%.

A labor market without collapse, but also without strength

The June report shows that the U.S. labor market is in a phase of clear slowdown. There are no signs of mass layoffs or a sharp deterioration in conditions, but it is becoming increasingly difficult to describe the market as strong. Companies are acting cautiously, new jobs are being created more slowly, and the decline in unemployment is partly the result of lower labor force participation.

The key takeaway from the report is therefore that the labor market is not collapsing, but it is losing resilience. For the Fed, this means less pressure from wages and employment, while for workers it means more challenging job-search conditions and limited improvement in real incomes.

data.title: Bitcoin Deepens Losses - Crypto Market Under Pressure
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • Bitcoin is under strong selling pressure, falling over 17% in a week and dropping below USD 60,000. The decline was intensified by USD 532 million in long liquidations on Binance, which triggered additional forced selling.
  • Market sentiment worsened after Strategy sold part of its bitcoin holdings. Although the sale was small — 32 BTC for USD 2.5 million — it raised concerns that the largest corporate bitcoin holder could make further sales in the future.
  • The broader crypto market is weak due to macro and demand concerns. Strong U.S. labor data reduced hopes for rate cuts, retail investors are shifting toward AI-related tech stocks, ETF inflows remain too small to support prices, and security concerns after the Zcash vulnerability further damaged trust.

Bitcoin has come under heavy selling pressure and has already lost more than 17 percent since the beginning of the week. On Friday, its price fell below the psychological barrier of USD 60,000, increasing investor concerns about a further deepening of the correction. Bitcoin has fallen below its 200-week SMA for the first time in three years. From its all-time high near USD 126,000, the leading cryptocurrency has already lost more than half of its value.

Long liquidations increase pressure on the market

The scale of the declines was amplified by the forced closure of leveraged positions. Over the past 24 hours, long positions worth USD 532 million were liquidated on the Binance exchange. Such a large wave of liquidations shows that many investors betting on a bitcoin rebound were forced to close their positions, which further increased selling pressure in the market.

This mechanism often deepens declines, as automatic liquidations lead to further sell orders. As a result, the market can move more sharply than would be implied solely by incoming macroeconomic data or the decisions of the largest investors.

Strategy’s Bitcoin sale weighed on sentiment

One of the factors worsening sentiment was the news that Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin and a company associated with Michael Saylor, had sold part of its bitcoin holdings. The company sold 32 bitcoins for USD 2.5 million. Although the transaction was small compared with the company’s overall portfolio, it carried significant symbolic weight.

It was only Strategy’s second bitcoin sale since it began making purchases in 2020. The company explained the decision as necessary to pay coupons to holders of preferred shares, but investors interpreted it as a possible weakening of the long-standing narrative of holding bitcoin indefinitely.

The market is primarily concerned that this small sale could foreshadow further, larger transactions in the future. This risk was highlighted by Peter Schiff, a well-known bitcoin critic, who stressed that the problem is not the scale of the current sale itself, but its potential consequences for investor confidence. Before this transaction, Strategy had reportedly purchased a total of 843,738 BTC for nearly USD 64 billion, which is why any change in the company’s strategy is being closely watched by the market.

Declines spread across the entire cryptocurrency market

Selling pressure was not limited to bitcoin. Ethereum fell by around 23 percent over the week to USD 1,555, while Solana lost about 22 percent, dropping to USD 63.75. Weakness was also visible in shares of companies linked to cryptocurrencies. Strategy’s stock fell by almost 10 percent, while Coinbase shares declined by 8.4 percent.

A modest positive signal came from inflows into U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs yesterday after 13 days of outflows. However, the scale of these inflows, amounting to just over USD 3 million, was too small to change the overall market picture. In practice, this means that institutional demand remains too weak to effectively stop the current sell-off.

Strong U.S. Data reduces hopes for rate cuts

Sentiment was also hurt by strong data from the U.S. labor market. Nonfarm payrolls rose by 172,000 in May, clearly above expectations. Such data reduces the likelihood of swift interest rate cuts in the United States, which is unfavorable for risk assets, including cryptocurrencies.

The strong labor market report weakened the narrative of imminent monetary policy easing, while bitcoin currently lacks a clear macroeconomic catalyst that could support a rebound.

Retail investors shift their attention to tech stocks

An additional problem for the crypto market is the outflow of some retail investors toward technology stocks, especially companies linked to artificial intelligence. Retail investors have largely left the cryptocurrency market and returned to equities, making it difficult to identify new sources of demand for bitcoin.

In an environment of weakening interest and a lack of fresh capital, every negative piece of news can trigger a stronger price reaction. This applies both to macroeconomic data and to decisions by major entities holding significant bitcoin reserves.

Security issues weaken trust in Crypto

The cryptocurrency market is also struggling with concerns over trust in the security of blockchain technology. Investors paid particular attention to a vulnerability in the Zcash network, after which the cryptocurrency’s price fell by more than 40 percent in a single day. Developers fixed the bug, but they were unable to clearly determine whether it had been exploited to create additional tokens.

This situation increased concerns that increasingly advanced artificial intelligence models may in the future help detect similar vulnerabilities in other cryptocurrency projects. For a market already under downward pressure, such information further worsens sentiment.

Lack of new sources of demand makes a rebound difficult

The current sell-off in bitcoin is the result of several negative factors overlapping: strong U.S. economic data, reduced expectations for interest rate cuts, investors shifting toward technology stocks, concerns about Strategy’s future actions, trust issues related to the security of some crypto projects, and the large scale of long liquidations in the leveraged instruments market.

Bitcoin remains under pressure, and the lack of clear new sources of demand means that a quick and sustained rebound may be difficult. The market appears weakened, and investors are watching increasingly closely to see whether the drop below USD 60,000 proves to be only a brief breach of an important level or a continuation of the downward trend that began in October 2025.

data.title: Chart alert: Bitcoin (BTC/USD) potential near-term bullish reversal emerging from the sub-$70K plunge
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key takeaways

  • Bitcoin plunged 16% over the past two weeks and briefly fell below the US$70,000 psychological level after MicroStrategy’s partial Bitcoin sale shattered the long-standing “never sell” narrative that had supported market sentiment.
  • Despite the sharp decline, several contrarian indicators suggest selling pressure may be nearing exhaustion, including an extremely oversold daily RSI reading, a surge in long-position liquidations, and signs of renewed accumulation by long-term holders.
  • Technical and on-chain metrics indicate the potential for a near-term bullish reversal above the key US$62,250 support level, with upside targets at US$74,880 and US$82,815 if buying momentum returns.

Let’s unpack the primary drivers and the technical setup.

The plunge and its fundamental catalysts

On Monday and Tuesday (1–2 June 2026), the cryptocurrency market absorbed a significant psychological blow. Spot BTC/USD tumbled sharply, slipping below the $70,000 psychological threshold and falling 16% over the past two weeks. It printed an intraday low of $65,370 on Wednesday, 3 June 2026.

The dominant driver of this week’s movement was the revelation that MicroStrategy, the world’s largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, sold a portion of its holdings for the first time in four years.

While the market impact is less about the absolute volume of the sale and more about the erosion of consensus, it effectively shattered founder Michael Saylor’s widely echoed “never sell” iron law.

This pivot disrupted the pricing anchor the market had historically relied on, injecting uncertainty and triggering a wave of defensive selling.

Technical and on-chain analysis suggesting a setup for a bullish reversal

The 16% plunge in BTC/USD has left it hovering just above its $62,250 key medium-term pivotal support and the lower boundary of its long-term secular ascending channel running from the December 2018 low.

In addition, the daily RSI momentum indicator hit a significant oversold level of 21.8 on Tuesday, 2 June 2026, its lowest since 5 February 2026, triggering a 35% rally in BTC/USD over the next three months.

Secondly, utilising TradingView’s crypto derivatives indicators for crypto futures and perpetual swaps, such as from Bybit, Binance, and OKX.

Aggregated long liquidation data (derived from various exchanges) spiked to $482 million on Tuesday, 2 June 2026, indicating that many leveraged long positions in Bitcoin futures and perpetual swaps were forced closed due to margin calls.

A similar rise in long liquidations ($481 million) also occurred on 5 February 2026, when capitulation led to a 35% rally in BTC/USD.

Thirdly, on-chain indicator: the percentage of 1-year active supply for Bitcoin has declined steadily over the past three weeks, from 40.3% on 23 April 2026 to 39.3% on Wednesday, 3 June 2026, at the time of writing.

Active supply 1-year measures the total number of unique cryptocurrency units that have moved at least once over the past 1 year. This metric tracks the portion of supply that has been involved in on-chain transactions during the trailing 365-day period.

A decreasing active supply often signals accumulation by long-term holders, a bullish condition for Bitcoin in the current context.

Hence, based on these factors, BTC/USD is now ripe for a potential near-term bullish reversal above the $62,250 key medium-term support, with intermediate resistance at $74,880. A clearance above it would signal a retest of the $82,815 medium-term resistance (also close to the 200-day moving average).

On the other hand, a daily close below $62,250 invalidates the recovery scenario and extends the corrective decline towards the $57,590/52,590 long-term pivotal support zone.

This clear difference shows that digital assets are not following the usual trends in the broader market, at least for now.

Cryptocurrencies have been stuck in a long period of relative sideways movement, unable to break out as some traders hoped.

This may have been frustrating for those looking for quick gains, but there are still some interesting technical signals to watch. The big question now is whether this slow price action is a warning sign or a chance to buy at a discount.

The digital asset market has shown resilience by bouncing off important moving averages, even though there has not been a big surge in retail trading.

data.title: Apple ahead of earnings: Record sales are only the beginning of the test
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • Apple faces expectations of $113.44 billion in quarterly revenue and earnings per share of $1.99.
  • Investors will assess whether strong iPhone sales and high-margin services can offset rising costs and supply constraints.
  • John Ternus’s first earnings report as CEO will put sustainable profitability and the holiday outlook in focus.

Apple is approaching its earnings release with expectations for quarterly revenue exceeding $113 billion. Following a strong first half of the calendar year, however, investors will be looking to see how much of that sales growth translates into a sustained improvement in profitability. The previous report showed that even record results require a careful reading of the footnotes: some of the profit came from tariff refunds.

November’s report will cover the quarter ended in September

The release scheduled for November 2 will cover Apple’s fourth fiscal quarter, which ended in September. This is an important distinction: the third fiscal quarter ended on June 27 and was reported in July. The upcoming results will include initial sales of the iPhone 18 Pro, while the October launch of the iPhone Duo will affect the following reporting period. Management’s commentary on the holiday season could therefore prove just as important as the historical figures.

The market expects revenue of more than $113 billion - tariff refunds boosted previous quarter

The analyst consensus calls for revenue of $113.44 billion and earnings per share of $1.99. That would represent year-over-year growth of approximately 10.7% and 7.6%, respectively. Apple’s management previously guided for quarterly revenue growth of 9–11% and a gross margin of 47–48%. Based on last year’s revenue of $102.47 billion, a simple calculation puts the implied revenue range at approximately $111.7–113.7 billion. The market forecast therefore sits near the upper end of that range. This raises the bar: meeting management’s guidance will not necessarily deliver a positive surprise for investors.

The record June quarter remains the benchmark. Apple generated approximately $109.4 billion in revenue, with diluted earnings per share of $2.02. However, the company disclosed that tariff refunds boosted earnings per share by 11 cents and gross margin by approximately 2 percentage points. Simply subtracting those benefits gives earnings per share of $1.91 and a gross margin of approximately 48.1%.

iPhone drives sales, but development is becoming more expensive

Sales were driven primarily by the iPhone, whose quarterly revenue rose approximately 22% to $54.25 billion. The Mac also performed strongly, with revenue increasing approximately 29% to $10.35 billion. Services generated $30.74 billion, up approximately 12% year over year. Their importance extends beyond revenue, however: the services gross margin was 75.6%, compared with 40.1% for products. This means the revenue mix has a significant impact on the company’s overall profitability.

At the same time, Apple must fund increasingly expensive development efforts. In the latest quarter, research and development spending rose 32% to $11.73 billion, while total operating expenses increased 23% to $19.08 billion. Both therefore grew faster than revenue. A key question in assessing the next set of results will be whether higher sales and a more favorable contribution from services are enough to cover rising expenditure.

Component availability remains a separate challenge. Speaking to Reuters after the July report, Tim Cook pointed to constraints on advanced chip production capacity. Memory costs also added pressure on profitability. This calls for caution when interpreting sales figures: an inability to deliver devices to willing buyers has different implications for the company’s future than weakening demand, even though both can limit revenue in the short term.

Apple shares closed at $347.10 on October 27, having reached an all-time high of $351.73 just two trading sessions earlier. The earnings release could determine whether the trend continues or investors shift into profit-taking mode. AAPL shares have gained more than 27.49% since the start of 2026.

John Ternus prepares for his first earnings report as CEO

The upcoming report will also be the first under John Ternus, who became Apple’s CEO on September 1. Tim Cook moved into the role of executive chairman of the board. The new leadership will therefore present the company’s outlook at a time when strong hardware sales are accompanied by rising costs and supply constraints. The most important test for Apple will be whether its improving results can be sustained. Beating the consensus by a few cents per share will say less than stable margins without one-off benefits, continued services growth, and the ability to deliver new devices during the holiday season. These factors will help determine whether the record June quarter signals a longer period of earnings growth.

data.title: Fed and ECB: a pause before further tightening
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • The Fed and ECB are likely to hold rates steady in October, while keeping December hikes on the table.
  • Persistent inflation and resilient growth support further monetary tightening.
  • French bond market tensions could constrain the ECB’s room to raise rates.
  • Lower energy prices and tighter financing conditions could reduce the need for additional hikes next year.
  • Central bank guidance will shape bond yields, while French fiscal risks could weigh on the euro.

The Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank are likely to leave interest rates unchanged at their October meetings. However, a pause would not necessarily mark the end of monetary tightening. Persistent inflation and resilient economic activity support the case for further increases in December, although tensions in the French government bond market could constrain the ECB.

Inflation remains too high

Price pressures on both sides of the Atlantic remain too strong for central banks to declare victory. In the US, annual PCE inflation stood at 3.4% in August, while the core measure reached 3.0%. In the euro area, headline inflation rose to 3.8%, with core inflation at 2.5%.

The risk that higher energy costs will feed through to other goods and services continues to complicate the return to target. Meanwhile, relatively resilient economic activity reduces the likelihood that weaker demand alone will quickly contain inflation.

The forecasts presented in the source material point to annualised US GDP growth of 3.5% in the third quarter and quarterly growth of 0.3% in the euro area. Such readings would give policymakers additional room to maintain a restrictive stance.

October favours caution

Despite these inflation risks, recent central bank communication suggests that caution will prevail in October. Following September’s rate increases, policymakers have reasons to assess their effects before taking further action. Geopolitical uncertainty and higher government bond yields also strengthen the case for a pause.

For the Federal Reserve, the proximity of the US midterm elections adds political sensitivity to the upcoming meeting. This could reinforce the appeal of waiting, although the inflation outlook remains the central consideration.

French debt tensions complicate the ECB’s decision

France presents an additional challenge for the ECB. The spread between French and German ten-year government bond yields has approached 175 basis points, reflecting concerns about public finances and the government’s ability to deliver fiscal consolidation.

Another rapid rate increase could raise borrowing costs further and intensify market tensions. A December hike therefore remains conditional on the French debt market avoiding a more serious deterioration.

December hikes remain the base case

A further 25 - basis - point increase by both central banks in December remains the base case. The outlook for additional tightening next year is less clear.

A normalisation of oil supplies from the Middle East could lower energy prices and gradually ease inflation. At the same time, elevated long - term bond yields are already tightening financing conditions, potentially reducing the need for further policy rate increases.

Guidance will shape the market response

Markets will focus on the guidance accompanying any October pause. A clear signal that December hikes remain on the table could limit declines in short-term bond yields.

For the euro, however, monetary policy expectations are only part of the picture. A further deterioration in French public finances could weigh on the currency even if the ECB maintains a hawkish message.

EUR/USD: Downtrend channel remains intact

There is no doubt that EUR/USD has been trading within a descending channel since February 2026. The latest upward correction ended around 1.1279, and the pair is now moving lower again. The pattern of lower highs and lower lows confirms that sellers remain in control.

The nearest support lies at 1.1115, last week’s low. A break below this level could pave the way towards the channel’s lower boundary, near 1.1000. Conversely, a recovery above 1.1279 could allow the correction to extend towards the 1.1340 area.

data.title: Meta Platforms (META) Q3 earnings preview: Can AI returns justify surging infrastructure spending?
data.description:
Referenced assets

Key takeaways

  • Advertising remains Meta’s core earnings engine, but investors increasingly want evidence that AI tools can lift monetisation and justify rapidly rising infrastructure spending.
  • Capex, margins and free cash flow are the key risks, especially if management signals another sizeable increase in AI-related spending heading into 2027.
  • Technically, 653.17 is the key support, while a break above 734.84 may reopen the path towards 777.60/793.70.

Ahead of Wednesday’s 21 Q3 2026 earnings, Meta Platforms (META) faces a critical test of whether its artificial intelligence (AI) investments are generating sufficient returns to justify surging infrastructure spending and maintain its valuation premium.

Meta is scheduled to release its results after the US market closes on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, followed by its earnings conference call at 4:30 pm Eastern Time.

Meta’s shares have retreated by 2.82% since the start of October through 19 October 2026, reflecting broader weakness in AI-related technology stocks, and Meta also underperformed several of its “Magnificent Seven” peers such as Alphabet (+1.76%), Apple (+3.82%), Tesla (+3.94%), Microsoft (+4.04%), and Amazon (+5.73%) (see Fig. 1).

Investors are now increasingly questioning whether rising capital expenditure will translate into sustainable earnings growth. The pullback follows mounting concerns over AI infrastructure financing, with semiconductor stocks also coming under selling pressure.

The street is expecting a 23.6% year-on-year increase in Meta’s Q3 revenue to US$63.34 billion and Q3 earnings per share of US$6.53.

In addition, options markets are pricing in roughly a ±7.1% earnings move, below Meta’s 10-year average peak earnings-day move of ±10.4%, suggesting a smaller-than-normal reaction.

Against this backdrop, Meta’s earnings reaction will likely hinge on advertising revenue growth, AI monetisation, operating margins, 2027 capital expenditure guidance and free cash flow.

Let’s now highlight seven fundamental factors that traders should be watching.

1. Advertising revenue growth: the core earnings driver

Meta’s advertising business, encompassing Facebook, Instagram, Reels and its other platforms, remains the principal source of revenue and cash generation.

Q3 consensus revenue of US$63.34 billion represents approximately 23.6% year-on-year growth, close to the upper end of management’s US$61 billion–US$64 billion guidance range.

Traders will focus on whether AI-powered advertising tools are improving recommendation quality, ad targeting and conversion rates sufficiently to support higher advertising prices and impressions.

2. AI monetisation: can Meta convert investment into revenue?

Meta’s AI monetisation strategy is increasingly important to its valuation, especially following the launch of its Muse AI assistant and continued investment in advertising automation.

Reports indicate that Muse has attracted more than two million daily users, although demonstrating meaningful revenue conversion remains a key challenge.

The market will monitor user adoption, potential subscription or commercialisation models, enterprise demand and the extent to which AI improvements contribute to the existing advertising business.

3. Capital expenditure: the biggest valuation risk

Based on current guidance mentioned in the Q2 2026 earnings results release in July, Meta’s full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance is US$130 billion–US$145 billion, including finance lease principal payments, an increase in the lower end of the prior guided spending range of US$125-US$145 billion, as it builds out AI computing infrastructure and data-centre capacity.

Importantly, the market is no longer focused solely on whether demand for AI infrastructure remains strong. Investors increasingly want evidence that the returns on these investments can justify their financing and operating costs.

S&P Global has recently highlighted growing concerns over hyperscaler AI-related financing commitments and the sustainability of infrastructure investments.

4. Operating margins and expense growth: profitability under pressure

Meta has guided full-year 2026 operating expenses of US$165 billion–US$169 billion, reflecting higher infrastructure costs, AI-related research and development, and legal expenses.

The critical issue is whether strong advertising revenue can continue to generate sufficient operating leverage to absorb these costs.

Management previously indicated that full-year 2026 operating income should exceed 2025 levels. Traders will assess whether that outlook remains achievable and, more importantly, how much further operating costs could increase in 2027.

5. Free cash flow: sustainability of the AI investment cycle

Free cash flow is emerging as one of the most important indicators of Meta’s financial flexibility.

Despite strong advertising profitability, Meta’s substantial capital expenditure commitments could continue to absorb an increasing share of operating cash flow.

Investors will be looking for signs that operating cash flow growth can eventually outpace infrastructure investment, allowing Meta to maintain its shareholder returns without compromising its AI ambitions.

6. Forward guidance: the most important post-earnings catalyst

Management’s fourth-quarter revenue outlook and preliminary 2027 spending expectations may have a greater influence on share-price performance than the reported Q3 numbers.

Traders will focus on whether advertising demand remains resilient heading into the year-end holiday season and whether Meta can maintain its growth trajectory amid higher infrastructure costs.

7. Market positioning and the broader AI sell-off

Meta’s results arrive at a sensitive juncture for US technology stocks.

The Nasdaq 100 and semiconductor sector have recently experienced significant weakness amid concerns over elevated AI infrastructure spending and the sustainability of the investment cycle.

Share-price implication: A stronger-than-expected earnings release could attract renewed buying interest in Meta and the wider AI-related technology sector. However, disappointing guidance could accelerate selling pressure, particularly if investors view Meta’s spending trajectory as further evidence of weakening returns on AI investment.

Fundamental bottom line: what matters most for traders

The market is increasingly distinguishing between companies benefiting from AI investment and those generating measurable financial returns from it.

For Meta, advertising remains the earnings engine, while AI infrastructure spending is the principal valuation risk.

The most bullish outcome would combine stronger advertising revenue, resilient operating margins and convincing evidence that AI adoption is translating into higher monetisation, without another substantial increase in projected expenditure.

Conversely, even an earnings beat may fail to support the share if management signals accelerating AI costs, weaker free cash flow or limited revenue visibility into 2027.

Let’s now focus on the multi-month outlook of Meta and key levels to watch from a technical analysis perspective

Technical analysis: Positive follow-through after bullish breakout from 13-month descending range

The price action of Meta staged a bullish breakout on 15 September 2026 from a four-week descending range, running from its current all-time high of 796.25, printed on 15 August 2025.

Thereafter, Meta rallied 16.3% to a 12-month high of 777.60 on 24 September 2026, then staged an 11% pullback while holding above its 50-day moving average in October.

The recent multi-month up move from the 30 July 2026 low to the 24 September 2026 high has been accompanied by higher-than-average volume relative to the prior multi-month rally of 21 April 2025 to 15 August 2025, suggesting that the bulls are likely in control (see Fig. 2).

The volatility-adjusted relative strength (VARS) of Meta against the Nasdaq 100 exchange-traded fund (QQQ) has trended upwards since 23 June 2026 and has remained above the centreline since 12 October 2026, a condition for further potential outperformance of Meta over the Nasdaq 100.

Watch the 653.17 key medium-term pivotal support (also the 50-day moving average) to maintain Meta’s potential multi-month uptrend phase. A clearance above 734.84 intermediate resistance (also the 20-day moving average) sees the medium-term resistance zone of 777.60/793.70 in the first step.

However, failure to hold and a daily close below 653.17 negate the bullish tone, suggesting a potential slide towards the key 200-day moving average, which acts as the next support at 626.68; a break below it would expose the major support of 540.90.

data.title: US Dollar strengthens as Fed rate hike fears grow
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • US dollar remains strong despite weakening consumer sentiment: The University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Index fell to 46.3 in October, signaling growing financial pressure on American households and concerns about future consumer spending.
  • Rising inflation expectations fuel speculation about further Fed rate hikes: US consumers expect inflation to reach 4.7% over the next 12 months, while markets price in an approximately 71% probability of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December.
  • High Treasury yields and geopolitical risks support the USD outlook: EURUSD remains near 1.1190, supported by expectations of restrictive monetary policy and safe-haven demand, although weakening consumption could limit further dollar gains.

The US dollar remains strong despite the latest macroeconomic data pointing to deteriorating financial conditions among American households. Rising inflation expectations, elevated Treasury yields, and concerns about further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve continue to support the US currency. Investors are increasingly focused on the risk of persistently high inflation, which could force the Fed to tighten monetary policy further, even as consumer spending weakens and economic growth slows.

US consumer sentiment falls to historically low levels

The latest data from the University of Michigan indicate a significant deterioration in US consumer sentiment in early October. The preliminary consumer sentiment index fell to 46.3 points, reaching its lowest level since May and coming in below economists' expectations of 47.6 points. Particularly concerning was the assessment of current economic conditions, with the corresponding index dropping from 50.9 to a record low of 44.7 points. Meanwhile, the consumer expectations index rose from 46.3 to 47.3 points, marking its first increase since July.

The deterioration in sentiment is primarily driven by rising living costs, high fuel prices, expensive borrowing, and signs of weakening labor market conditions. Lower-income households are experiencing the greatest pressure, as spending on essential goods and services accounts for a substantial share of their budgets. Additionally, consumers' assessment of durable goods buying conditions fell to an all-time low, reflecting their declining purchasing power.

Despite weak sentiment, US consumer spending remains relatively strong, supported by the labor market and previous increases in financial asset prices. However, growing evidence suggests that consumption could slow in the coming months. Only 31% of respondents say they intend to maintain their current spending levels over the next year, while more than half plan to cut back on purchases, including spending on cars, restaurants, and vacations.

Rising inflation expectations increase pressure on the Fed

From a foreign exchange market perspective, the renewed increase in inflation expectations is particularly significant. American consumers expect prices to rise by 4.7% over the next 12 months, compared with 4.6% in September. Over the longer-term horizon of five to ten years, expected average annual inflation stands at 3.5%, remaining well above the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target.

Persistent price pressures are putting the Fed in an increasingly difficult position. On the one hand, deteriorating consumer sentiment and signs of a slowdown in the labor market argue for caution when considering further interest rate increases. On the other hand, elevated inflation expectations could make it more difficult to bring inflation back to target, limiting the central bank's room to ease monetary policy.

For the US dollar, this creates a potentially favorable environment. If the Fed is forced to maintain restrictive financial conditions for longer than previously anticipated, US assets could remain attractive to international investors. At the same time, the growing risk of a combination of weak economic growth and persistent inflation is increasing uncertainty about the future health of the US economy.

Markets increasingly price in further interest rate hikes

One of the most important factors supporting the dollar is the shift in expectations regarding the Federal Reserve's future policy decisions. Following September's 25-basis-point interest rate hike, investors are increasingly pricing in the possibility of further monetary tightening before the end of 2026.

According to CME FedWatch data, the probability of another interest rate hike at the Fed's October meeting stood at approximately 19%. This indicates that keeping interest rates unchanged remains the dominant scenario. Expectations for December, however, paint a markedly different picture, with markets assigning an approximately 71% probability to an interest rate increase.

These expectations suggest that investors increasingly view a potential pause in October as temporary rather than as the definitive end of the monetary tightening cycle. Further support for this scenario comes from the minutes of the Fed's September meeting, which indicate that most central bank officials acknowledge the possibility that additional interest rate increases may be necessary before the end of the year.

The shift in monetary policy expectations has a direct impact on the foreign exchange market. The prospect of higher interest rates tends to push US Treasury yields higher, increasing the attractiveness of dollar-denominated assets. At the same time, it limits the potential for dollar depreciation, particularly against currencies issued by countries whose central banks may pursue less restrictive monetary policies.

Dollar benefits from high treasury yields and geopolitical uncertainty

Additional support for the USD comes from heightened geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. The conflict and associated disruptions to energy markets are contributing to rising commodity prices, increasing the risk of persistently elevated inflation. At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty periodically boosts demand for the US dollar, which remains one of the world's most important reserve currencies.

As a result, the US currency is receiving support from two directions. On the one hand, investors expect interest rates to remain elevated. On the other, they are seeking liquid assets amid heightened market uncertainty. The combination of these factors could limit the extent of dollar corrections, even in response to weaker economic data.

Weakening consumer spending could threaten further USD gains

Despite a monetary policy environment that remains favorable for the dollar, there is a growing risk that deteriorating financial conditions among American households will begin to weigh on economic growth prospects. Consumer spending remains the primary engine of the US economy, meaning that a significant slowdown could change expectations regarding future Fed decisions.

A particularly important question will be whether consumers' stated intentions to reduce spending are reflected in retail sales and personal consumption data. So far, weak consumer sentiment has not translated into an equally sharp decline in actual spending. However, persistently high living and borrowing costs could gradually undermine household resilience.

For the foreign exchange market, the key issue will be the relationship between the pace of the economic slowdown and the persistence of inflation. If price pressures remain elevated, the Fed may continue pursuing restrictive monetary policy despite weaker economic activity data, which should support the dollar. However, if labor market conditions deteriorate and consumer spending weakens more sharply than expected, investors may begin scaling back their bets on further interest rate hikes.

US Dollar outlook: Will the USD continue to strengthen?

In the short term, the macroeconomic environment continues to favor a relatively strong US dollar. Rising inflation expectations, elevated Treasury yields, and the market-implied probability of a December interest rate hike all point to sustained demand for the US currency. Geopolitical uncertainty provides an additional source of support for the USD by increasing investor interest in safer and more liquid assets.

At the same time, the scope for further dollar appreciation will depend on upcoming macroeconomic releases. Particular attention will be paid to CPI and PCE inflation figures, labor market conditions, and consumer spending data. These indicators will help determine whether the US economy can sustain growth despite high borrowing costs and deteriorating household sentiment.

Over the coming weeks, the balance of factors remains in favor of the dollar, although the risk of a trend reversal is gradually increasing. As long as investors continue to anticipate further Fed interest rate hikes, the US currency should benefit from relatively high Treasury yields and capital inflows. However, increasingly weak consumer sentiment suggests that the resilience of the US economy could face a serious test.

In the medium term, the direction of the USD will depend primarily on whether persistent inflation continues to necessitate restrictive monetary policy or whether an intensifying economic slowdown prompts markets to begin pricing in interest rate cuts once again.

data.title: Fed is moving closer to a september rate hike
data.description:
Referenced assets

  • A September Fed rate hike is increasingly likely, with market-implied odds rising above 85% after stronger-than-expected core inflation data.
  • Inflation risks remain elevated, driven by persistent price pressures, higher oil prices, strong economic growth and rising consumer inflation expectations.
  • Further rate hikes may follow, while tighter monetary policy could also intensify political tensions between the Federal Reserve and Donald Trump.

The Federal Reserve is facing growing pressure to raise interest rates at its September 15–16 meeting. The latest U.S. inflation data came in above expectations, while the American economy remains strong enough to leave the Fed with increasingly fewer arguments for keeping rates at their current level.

Core CPI rose 0.3% month over month in August, exceeding economists’ forecasts. The data confirmed that despite more than five years of efforts to bring price growth under control, inflationary pressures in the United States remain elevated. Of particular concern to the Fed is the lack of sufficiently clear progress toward its 2% inflation target.

The market reaction was swift. The probability of a rate hike at the September meeting rose from around 70% to more than 85%. Investors also began assigning a greater probability to a second increase by December. Following the release of the data, economists at institutions including TD Bank and JPMorgan revised their forecasts, pointing to a higher likelihood of monetary policy tightening.

Brent crude increase rite hike probability

A record increase in wireless phone service prices accounted for a significant share of August’s rise in core inflation. This suggests that part of the acceleration may have been driven by a one-off factor. However, the Fed must also consider other sources of price pressure that could prove far more persistent.

One of them is rising oil prices. Brent crude climbed as high as $109 a barrel on Thursday. More expensive energy could gradually feed into transportation and production costs and, ultimately, into the prices of other goods and services. Strong demand in the economy, partly driven by the rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, is another factor sustaining inflationary pressure.

A rate hike has also become more likely because of earlier comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. He has stressed that core inflation has not improved sufficiently and that the central bank will have to act unless convincing evidence emerges that inflation is moving sustainably back toward the 2% target. Against that backdrop, leaving rates unchanged could be seen as inconsistent with his earlier statements.

Some economists therefore believe that the September meeting is about more than just the level of interest rates. The credibility of the Fed chair may also be at stake. Bloomberg Economics says the market is now clearly expecting a rate hike and that failing to deliver one could weaken Warsh’s position.

Inflation and higher oil prices increase pressure on the Fed

Support for higher interest rates had been growing within the Federal Reserve even before the latest inflation figures were released. The central bank has left rates unchanged at five meetings this year, but in July three members voted in favor of a 25-basis-point increase. Two other Fed officials who did not have voting rights at the time expressed a similar view.

The strength of the U.S. economy also supports the case for tighter monetary policy. Unemployment remains low and stable, while some Fed officials are beginning to conclude that the current level of interest rates is restraining demand less than previously assumed.

If that assessment proves correct, the central bank could decide that at least some of the rate cuts implemented in 2025 need to be reversed. The Fed lowered rates by a total of 75 basis points that year. With economic growth remaining strong and inflation elevated, current borrowing costs may be too low to curb price pressures effectively.

Consumer surveys are also sending worrying signals. According to the University of Michigan, consumers’ one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.6% in September from 4.0% a month earlier. Moreover, for the first time since 2023, a majority of respondents expect interest rates to rise over the next year.

Rising inflation expectations are particularly important for the Fed. If households and businesses begin to assume that high inflation will persist for longer, those expectations could influence decisions on wages, prices and spending. That, in turn, would make returning inflation to the Fed’s target even more difficult.

Markets are pricing in further rate hikes

A growing number of economists believe that a potential September move may not be the final rate hike of the year. Markets have also started pricing in the possibility of another increase before year-end. The main argument is the strength of the economy, which could expand this quarter at a pace well above its long-term trend.

Such strong growth combined with low unemployment increases the risk that demand will remain too robust for inflation to return quickly to 2%. If oil prices also remain high, the Fed could find itself forced to tighten monetary policy more aggressively.

The conflict in Iran remains another significant source of uncertainty. Its impact on the oil market could add to inflationary pressures in the U.S. economy. If higher energy costs prove persistent and begin feeding through to other categories of prices, the case for further rate hikes will become even stronger.

The Fed’s decision could intensify its conflict with Donald Trump

Tighter monetary policy would have political as well as economic consequences. Donald Trump has been calling for lower interest rates, meaning that a rate hike would likely further increase tensions between the White House and the Federal Reserve.

The Fed therefore finds itself in an increasingly difficult position. On the one hand, it must respond to persistent inflation, rising inflation expectations, high oil prices and a strong economy. On the other, higher interest rates mean increased borrowing costs for households and businesses and could trigger another wave of political pressure on the central bank.

The latest data have nevertheless shifted the balance of arguments clearly toward tighter monetary policy. Until recently, the main question was whether the Fed would raise rates in September. Increasingly, the more important question is whether a September move would be a one-off adjustment or the beginning of a longer tightening cycle that reverses some—or even all—of the rate cuts implemented in 2025.
